456.title: Indra goes back
456.hook: Indra and Virochana look into the water for the self, and only Indra goes back
456.carry: viveka: telling the self from what it sees
456.tomorrow: The serpent who came to teach
456.howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, discernment between awareness and what it is aware of is the central means of liberation, cultivated over years through study, the ethical disciplines and meditation, usually under a teacher's guidance.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: apavarga, and your line, bhoga and apavarga: the world is there for both, experience and freedom. Today, a king of the gods who wouldn't stop at the first answer.
screen: `BHOGA AND APAVARGA: THE WORLD IS FOR BOTH — EXPERIENCE AND FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Two students arrive at a teacher's door with firewood in their hands, the old sign of asking to learn. One is Indra, king of the gods. The other is Virochana, king of the demons. Both have heard the teacher, Prajapati, speak of a self that never ages, never dies, never grieves, and both want it. For thirty-two years they live with him and wait. Then Prajapati tells them to put on their finest clothes and look into a pan of water. That, he says, is the self. Both walk away happy. Only one of them comes back.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ONE TEACHER.` → `LOOK INTO THE WATER.` → `ONLY ONE COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Chandogya Upanishad. Virochana goes home and teaches the demons that the body is the self: dress it, feed it, serve it. Indra gets partway home and stops. If the body is dressed up, the reflection is dressed up. If the body is hurt, the reflection is hurt. If the body dies, this self dies too. That can't be the deathless one. So he goes back. Thirty-two more years, and a new answer: the one who dreams. Again he doubts, and goes back. Thirty-two more, and another answer. He goes back once more. A hundred and one years in all, before Prajapati tells him plainly: the body is mortal, a home for the self, which has no body at all. Hindus call that self the atman. You can hear this week's book in that story. Patanjali names the remedy for suffering in sutra 2.26: viveka, discernment, telling the seer from the seen, the self from everything it looks at, including the body and the mind. And he adds one word: aviplava, unwavering. Virochana had a flash and stopped. Indra kept going until the seeing held. Sutra 2.28 says how it grows: practice the limbs of yoga, and as impurity dwindles, the light of knowledge shines all the way to discernment. Day to day, viveka sounds small: this is a mood, not me. This is a thought, not the one watching it. Said once, it's a flash. Said every day, it's Indra going back.
screen: `VIROCHANA STOPS AT THE REFLECTION.` · `INDRA GOES BACK, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `VIVEKA — TELLING APART.` · `AVIPLAVA — UNWAVERING.` · then, large: `VIVEKA.`

segments.voice: Count the out-breaths from one to ten, then start again; if you keep a mala, move one bead with each breath instead. When a thought pulls you off count, notice it plainly, a thought, not the one watching it, and go back to one. Losing count isn't failure: noticing is the discernment, and coming back, again and again, like Indra, is the steadiness.
Aviplava. Unwavering discernment between seer and seen, held so steady it stops wavering.
screen: `AVIPLAVA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: viveka, telling the self from what it sees. Virochana stopped at the reflection; Indra kept going back. See you tomorrow.

457.title: The serpent who came to teach
457.hook: a tiny snake falls into a praying woman's hands and grows up to teach yoga's eight limbs
457.carry: eight limbs, and ethics come first
457.howItsDone: Many yoga classes open with a chant bowing to Patanjali, often pictured with a serpent's coil and hoods; classical teaching presents the eight limbs of 2.29 as the framework of the whole practice, starting with the restraints and observances.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: aviplava, unwavering, and your line, viveka: telling the self from what it sees. Virochana stopped at the reflection, Indra kept going back. Today, the teacher behind this book.
screen: `VIVEKA: TELLING THE SELF FROM WHAT IT SEES — INDRA GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: A woman named Gonika stands at a river at sunrise, offering water to the sun from her cupped hands. For years she has prayed for someone to pass her learning on to. As she lifts her hands, something tiny drops into them: a little snake. It becomes a child. A traditional story, still told in yoga schools, says this was Shesha, the great serpent Vishnu rests on, come down to teach. Fallen, pata, into folded hands, anjali. Patanjali.
screen: `A WOMAN OFFERS WATER TO THE SUN.` → `A TINY SNAKE FALLS INTO HER HANDS.` → `PATA, ANJALI.`

segments.voice: That's why statues of Patanjali often show a sage whose lower body is a serpent's coil, with hoods spread over his head. Many yoga classes still open with an old verse that bows to him with folded hands, the sage who cleared the mind with yoga, speech with grammar and the body with medicine. Many teachers read the story as a picture of how Hindus hold this book: yoga as a gift that came down to clean a person all the way through. So what did he teach? Sutra 2.29 lists the eight limbs, ashtanga. Ashta, eight; anga, limb. Yama, the restraints: how you treat others. Niyama, the observances: how you keep yourself. Asana, the seat. Pranayama, the breath. Pratyahara, the senses drawing back. Dharana, concentration. Dhyana, meditation. Samadhi, absorption. Listen to the direction. It starts with other people and moves inward, until only the object shines. Teachers read the shape two ways: a ladder, ethics first and then body and mind; or limbs, which grow together, like a child's arms and legs. Either way, the proportion is plain. Ethics first, twice. Posture, one word out of eight. So when a studio timetable says Ashtanga, six p.m., bring water, that class is a modern tradition of its own. The word behind it is older, and in the sutra it begins with how you treat the people in the room.

segments.voice: Walk the eight in miniature: a moment of goodwill toward someone, contentment with this exact moment, a steady and easy seat, a slightly longer breath, sounds and sights left in the background. Then rest your attention on one point, maybe the breath at the nostrils, let it flow without breaks, and if the point fills everything, let it. If it doesn't, that's normal.
Ashtanga. The eight parts of yoga in sutra 2.29, from how you treat others all the way in to absorption.

458.title: The hunter and the birds
458.hook: Valmiki sees a hunter kill one of two birds, and his grief becomes the first verse
458.howItsDone: In classical yoga teaching the five yamas come before any posture or breathing practice; in Hindu homes ahimsa is a common reason families eat vegetarian food, especially on holy days, and renunciants may take the yamas as formal vows.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashtanga, eight limbs, and ethics come first, taught by the serpent who came down. Today, the first limb.
screen: `ASHTANGA — ETHICS FIRST.`

segments.voice: A sage named Valmiki walks down to the Tamasa river to bathe. In a tree nearby, two krauncha birds, a pair, are calling to each other. A hunter's arrow strikes one, and it falls to the ground. Its mate circles it, crying. Valmiki is so moved that words burst out of him: hunter, may you find no rest for endless years, for you killed one of a pair lost in love. Then he stops, startled. The words came out in a perfect meter. The Ramayana says his grief, shoka, became verse, shloka. The first poem.
screen: `TWO BIRDS ON A BRANCH.` → `ONE ARROW.` → `GRIEF BECOMES VERSE.`

segments.voice: The Ramayana tells this as the moment its own poetry began: with a man who couldn't bear harm done to a bird. That's the first limb of yoga in a story. Sutra 2.30 names the five yamas, the restraints. Ahimsa, non-harm. Satya, truthfulness. Asteya, not stealing. Brahmacharya, restraint, which the classical commentary reads as sexual restraint and many householder teachers read as faithfulness and moderation. And aparigraha, not grasping. The commentary traditionally credited to Vyasa makes the key move: ahimsa is the root, and the other four are there to serve it. Even truth serves non-harm: speech should be for the good of all beings, and a true sentence spoken to wound only looks like virtue. Sutra 2.31 raises the stakes. These five become the great vow, mahavrata, when they hold everywhere, with no exceptions for kind of being, place, time or occasion. The commentary's example of a limited vow sounds like Valmiki's river: a fisherman who says, I'll harm only fish. The great vow has no fine print. The bird counts too. You'll see this root at Hindu tables. Many Hindus, though not all, eat vegetarian food because of ahimsa, and many who eat meat keep it off the plate on holy days. The word traveled far: Jains and Buddhists hold it dear, and Gandhi carried it into politics. In the sutras it's quieter. It's page one.
screen: `VALMIKI'S GRIEF.` · `FIVE RESTRAINTS.` · `AHIMSA IS THE ROOT.` · `THE GREAT VOW HAS NO FINE PRINT.` · then, large: `AHIMSA FIRST.`

segments.voice: Notice the tone of the voice in your head, and whether a thought arrives with a little harshness, toward yourself or someone else. Don't argue with it; just soften the tone, the way you'd lower your voice near a sleeping child, and let the thought go on its way. Then rest with the breath until the next one.
Yama. The restraints, the first limb of yoga: non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint and non-grasping.

459.title: Parvati's fire
459.hook: Parvati gives up even leaves in her tapas for Shiva, and the second limb turns to how you keep yourself
459.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes and yoga lineages, the niyamas shape daily life: bathing before worship, fasts such as Monday fasts for Shiva, Ekadashi for Vishnu or the Teej fast that remembers Parvati, reading scripture or repeating a mantra, and offering one's actions to God; the young, the old and the unwell are usually excused from fasting.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: yama, the five restraints, with ahimsa, non-harm, as the root. Valmiki grieved for one bird. Today, the second limb.
screen: `YAMA — AHIMSA IS THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Parvati, daughter of the Himalaya, has set her heart on Shiva, and Shiva sits in meditation, unmoved. So, in the poet Kalidasa's telling, she puts away her jewels and goes into the mountains to do tapas. In summer she sits between four fires with the sun blazing overhead. In winter she stands in icy water. She lives on fallen leaves, then gives up even those, and people call her Aparna, the one without even a leaf. One day a young ascetic arrives, sits down beside her, and starts to make fun of Shiva.
screen: `PARVATI GOES TO THE MOUNTAINS.` → `FOUR FIRES AND THE SUN.` → `NOT EVEN A LEAF.`

segments.voice: He's smeared with ash, the visitor says. He wears snakes, haunts the cremation ground, rides an old bull. Why waste yourself on him? Parvati flushes, defends Shiva, and gets up to leave. And the visitor takes his true form. It was Shiva all along. From today, he tells her, I'm yours, bought by your tapas. Tapas means heat, and it sits at the center of today's limb. Sutra 2.32 names the niyamas, the observances: how you keep yourself, where the yamas face other people. Shaucha, cleanliness, outer and inner. Santosha, contentment. Tapas, discipline, which the classical commentary describes as bearing the pairs: hunger and thirst, heat and cold. Svadhyaya, study, or repeating a mantra like Om. And ishvara-pranidhana, offering everything you do to God. The last three, discipline, study, surrender, are the same three Patanjali gave at the start of book two: kriya yoga, the practice for people who aren't born calm. Now notice what Parvati's heat is for. It isn't punishment, and it isn't a show. It's devotion, lived in the body. That's why, in many Hindu homes, people keep fasts: on Mondays for Shiva, on Ekadashi for Vishnu, and many women keep the Teej fast, which remembers Parvati's tapas. A fast like that isn't a diet. It's heat, offered.
screen: `THE VISITOR MOCKS SHIVA.` · `IT WAS SHIVA ALL ALONG.` · `THE SECOND FIVE: HOW YOU KEEP YOURSELF.` · `TAPAS MEANS HEAT.` · then, large: `HEAT, OFFERED.`

segments.voice: Give this sit a little heat: stay still through one itch or one urge to check your phone, without fighting it. Then touch the rest of the five lightly: a clean, cool breath, contentment with this seat, a slow Om or a name of God you love, repeated in your mind. If you pray, offer the sit to God. If you don't, simply let go of trying.
Niyama. The observances, the second limb of yoga: cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study and surrender to Ishvara.
screen: `NIYAMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: tapas, discipline offered to God. Parvati's heat wasn't punishment; it was devotion. Day four fifty-nine, done.

460.title: The deer in the hermitage
460.hook: hermits stop a king's arrow, and in their grove the deer don't run
460.carry: where non-harm takes root, hostility drops
460.howItsDone: Hindu stories, from Kalidasa's Shakuntala to the Puranas, often describe hermitages as places where wild animals live at peace, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present the fruits of 2.35–2.39 as signs that the restraints have taken root, whether read as powers or as the natural results of an ethical life.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: niyama, the second limb, and tapas, discipline offered to God, in Parvati's fire. Today, what grows when the restraints take root.
screen: `TAPAS — HEAT, OFFERED.`

segments.voice: A king is out hunting, standing in his chariot, an arrow already on the string. Ahead of him a deer runs for its life, glancing back over its shoulder. He's about to shoot when voices call out: king, stop! This deer belongs to the hermitage. Hermits step into the path with their hands raised. And the king, the most powerful man in the forest, lowers his bow. This is the opening of Kalidasa's play Shakuntala. As King Dushyanta walks on into the grove, he notices something strange: here, the deer don't run from the sound of his chariot.
screen: `AN ARROW ON THE STRING.` → `THIS DEER BELONGS TO THE HERMITAGE.` → `THE KING LOWERS HIS BOW.`

segments.voice: Hindu stories picture hermitages this way again and again: places where animals stop being afraid and hunters stop hunting. Patanjali puts that picture into one sutra. Sutra 2.35: when someone is grounded in non-harm, hostility is given up in their presence. Not their own hostility. Everyone else's. Grounded means firmly established, standing on it. The classical commentary says all creatures near such a person abandon their enmity. Then come the fruits of the other four restraints. Grounded in truth, your words don't fail. Grounded in not stealing, jewels come near. Grounded in restraint, vigor. Grounded in not grasping, insight into the how and why of your births. How should these be read? Within the tradition, some take them as real powers that come with mastery. Others read them as the natural shape of a life: people drop their guard around someone who will never hurt them, and trust the word of someone who never lies. Both readings agree on one thing. The fruit doesn't come from chasing the fruit. The hermits didn't train the deer to be brave. Their way of living did it, over years. You may have met someone like that: a grandmother who sits down at a dinner that's about to turn into a fight, asks someone about their garden, and the air changes. She isn't performing calm. She stopped carrying a weapon a long time ago.

461.title: Dhruva's handful of husks
461.hook: Dhruva does tapas for a throne higher than anyone's, then finds his wish was husks
461.carry: santosha: nothing is higher than enough
461.tomorrow: The serpent who holds the world
461.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often single out santosha as a daily practice of accepting what is at hand; Dhruva's story is a favorite with Hindu children, many Hindus call the pole star Dhruva, and some link contentment to offering food to God before eating and receiving it back as prasad.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: where non-harm takes root, hostility drops, like deer that don't run at a hermitage.
screen: `AROUND NON-HARM, HOSTILITY DROPS.`

segments.voice: A little boy, Dhruva, five years old, tries to climb onto his father's lap. His half-brother is already sitting there. His stepmother pulls him away: you weren't born from me, she says, so you don't belong there. If you want that seat, pray to God to be born as my son. Dhruva runs crying to his mother. She doesn't argue. She tells him only the Lord can take away a pain like this. So the boy walks into the forest, alone, to ask God for a throne higher than anyone's.
screen: `PULLED OFF HIS FATHER'S LAP.` → `INTO THE FOREST, AGE FIVE.` → `A THRONE HIGHER THAN ANYONE'S.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Narada meets him on the road and gives him a mantra: om namo bhagavate vasudevaya. Dhruva repeats it for months, living on fruit, then leaves, then water, then air. And Vishnu appears. The boy gets what he came for: a kingdom, and a place in the sky that never moves, the pole star. But the Bhagavata says something surprising. Dhruva wasn't happy with his own wish. He felt like someone who had pleased an emperor and asked him for a handful of husks. Many teachers read it this way: he'd met the Lord, and he'd asked for a chair. That's sutra 2.42 in a story. From contentment, santosha, comes unsurpassed happiness: anuttama, nothing higher, nothing above it. The classical commentary quotes an old verse: whatever pleasure desire brings in this world, and whatever great pleasure there is in heaven, together they aren't worth a sixteenth of the happiness that comes when craving ends. And contentment here isn't settling. The commentary calls it not wanting more than what's at hand. The wanting that began on his father's lap was the wound, not the missing chair. Around this line, Patanjali gives the other observances' fruits: from study, meeting your chosen deity; from surrender to Ishvara, samadhi. Many Hindus still call the pole star Dhruva. Point to it tonight, and you're pointing at a boy who found something with nothing above it.
screen: `A MANTRA, AND MONTHS IN THE FOREST.` · `VISHNU APPEARS.` · `A HANDFUL OF HUSKS.` · `NOT WORTH A SIXTEENTH PART.` · then, large: `SANTOSHA.`

segments.voice: Notice one thing that's already here and already enough: the breath arriving without being asked, the chair holding you up, a little warmth in your hands. When the mind starts listing what's missing, notice the list and come back to what's enough. If you pray, you can repeat a name of God slowly, as Dhruva did. You don't have to feel blissful; just let enough be enough.
Anuttama, unsurpassed, nothing higher. Sutra 2.42: from contentment, santosha, a happiness with nothing above it.

462.title: The serpent who holds the world
462.hook: Shesha holds up the whole earth without strain, and Patanjali's seat is steady and easy
462.carry: asana: a seat both steady and easy
462.howItsDone: In the Yoga Sutras, asana is the seated posture for meditation, steady and easy; in puja the asana is the seat or mat the worshipper sits on, Hindus who meditate or do japa often sit cross-legged on one, and modern posture classes draw on later hatha yoga traditions.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: anuttama, nothing higher, and your line, santosha: nothing is higher than enough, as Dhruva found when he met the Lord.
screen: `SANTOSHA: NOTHING IS HIGHER THAN ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Between one age of the world and the next, the Puranas say, there is only ocean, and on it floats a vast serpent with a thousand hoods, coiled like a bed. Vishnu rests on him. His name is Shesha, also called Ananta, the endless, and in the Vishnu Purana he carries the whole earth on his hoods: mountains, seas, cities, everyone. He doesn't strain. He doesn't drop it. Only when he yawns, the text says, does the earth tremble. Remember him from the start of the week? The tradition says Patanjali was Shesha come down. So what did the serpent teach about sitting?
screen: `AN OCEAN BETWEEN WORLDS.` → `A SERPENT WITH A THOUSAND HOODS.` → `HOLDING THE EARTH, NO STRAIN.`

segments.voice: Three short sutras. Sutra 2.46: sthira sukham asanam. Sthira, steady. Sukha, easy, comfortable. Asana, seat, from a root meaning to sit. Not rigid. Not slumped. Both at once. Sutra 2.47 says how: by relaxing effort, and letting the mind rest in the endless, ananta. Some commentators hear the serpent in that word: Shesha, holding the world steady and easy, is a picture of the seat. Sutra 2.48 gives the result: then you're not knocked about by the pairs, heat and cold, comfort and discomfort. That's all it says. The classical commentary adds a few names of seats, the lotus and the hero's seat among them, but no sequence and no instructions. The long lists of postures belong to later hatha yoga texts and to modern teachers. That doesn't make them wrong. It shows what Patanjali was after: a body quiet enough to forget, so the inner limbs can begin. Hindus still use the word this way. In puja, the asana is the seat or small mat you sit on before the shrine, and a steady, easy seat is where japa and prayer happen. Now look back over the week. Indra kept going back. The serpent came down to teach eight limbs. Valmiki grieved for one bird. Parvati's fire. Deer that don't run. Dhruva's husks. And today, a seat. A week of the outer limbs, and almost none of it was about the body.
screen: `STHIRA, SUKHA: STEADY, EASY.` · `RELAX THE EFFORT, REST IN THE ENDLESS.` · `NO LONGER KNOCKED BY THE PAIRS.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `ASANA.`

segments.voice: Find a seat, chair, cushion or floor, and make it steady: the spine rising a little, the base settling down. Then make it easy: drop the shoulders, unclench the jaw, soften the hands, and let whatever's under you do the holding, the way Shesha holds the world. When an itch or ache asks for attention, notice it like weather.
Asana. The seat, the third limb of yoga, which Patanjali describes in three words: steady and comfortable.
